entries.text: The perimeter is the total length of the boundary around a 2D shape, found by adding up the lengths of all its sides. It is measured in ordinary length units such as cm or m.
entries.example: A rectangle 5 cm by 3 cm has perimeter 5 + 3 + 5 + 3 = 16 cm, or 2 × (5 + 3) = 16 cm.

entries.text: The circumference is the perimeter of a circle: the distance once all the way around its edge. Formula: C = 2πr = πd, where r is the radius and d is the diameter.
entries.example: A circle with radius 3 cm has circumference 2 × π × 3 ≈ 18.85 cm.

entries.text: The radius is the distance from the center of a circle or sphere out to any point on its edge or surface. It is half the diameter, so r = d ÷ 2.
entries.example: A circle with diameter 10 cm has radius 10 ÷ 2 = 5 cm.

entries.text: The diameter is the straight distance across a circle that passes through its center. It is twice the radius, so d = 2r.
entries.example: A circle with radius 4 m has diameter 2 × 4 = 8 m.

entries.text: Area is how much flat space a 2D shape covers, measured in square units such as cm² or m². Formulas: rectangle A = l × w, triangle A = ½ × b × h, circle A = πr².
entries.example: A triangle with base 6 m and height 4 m has area ½ × 6 × 4 = 12 m².

entries.text: Volume is how much 3D space a solid or container fills, measured in cubic units such as cm³ or m³. Formulas: box V = l × w × h, cylinder V = πr²h, sphere V = (4/3)πr³.
entries.example: A box measuring 4 cm × 3 cm × 2 cm has volume 4 × 3 × 2 = 24 cm³.

entries.text: Surface area is the total area of the outer surface of a 3D solid, measured in square units such as cm². For a box it is the sum of its six face areas: SA = 2(lw + lh + wh).
entries.example: A cube with side 2 cm has surface area 6 × 2² = 24 cm².

entries.text: A radian is an angle unit based on the circle itself: one radian is the angle that cuts off an arc exactly as long as the radius. A full turn is 2π radians, so π radians = 180°.
entries.example: To convert 90° to radians: 90 × π ÷ 180 = π/2 ≈ 1.571 rad.

entries.text: A degree (°) is the usual unit for measuring angles, with a full turn equal to 360°. A right angle is 90° and a straight angle is 180°.
entries.example: The three angles of a triangle add to 180°, so if two are 60° and 70°, the third is 180 − 60 − 70 = 50°.

entries.text: An angle is the amount of turn between two lines or rays that meet at a point called the vertex. It is measured in degrees (°) or radians.
entries.example: A square corner is a 90° angle, and half a turn is a 180° angle.

entries.text: Similar triangles have the same shape but possibly different sizes: their matching angles are equal, and every matching side is multiplied by the same scale factor.
entries.example: A 3-4-5 triangle and a 6-8-10 triangle are similar, since each side of the second is 2 times the matching side of the first.

entries.text: In any right triangle, the square of the hypotenuse equals the sum of the squares of the other two sides: a² + b² = c², where c is the hypotenuse. Use it to find a missing side when the other two are known.
entries.example: If the legs are 3 cm and 4 cm, then c² = 9 + 16 = 25, so c = √25 = 5 cm.

entries.text: Arc length is the distance along a curved piece of a circle's edge. It equals (θ ÷ 360) × 2πr when θ is in degrees, or s = rθ when θ is in radians.
entries.example: A 90° arc on a circle with radius 4 cm has length (90 ÷ 360) × 2π × 4 = 2π ≈ 6.28 cm.

entries.text: The original amount of money borrowed or invested, before any interest is added. The first period's interest is calculated from this starting amount.
entries.example: Borrow $2,000 at 5% a year: the principal is $2,000, and the first year's interest is $100.

entries.text: The percentage of the principal charged on a loan or earned on savings over one period, usually a year. Interest for one period = principal × rate, so 5% means 0.05 × the principal.
entries.example: $2,000 at 5% a year: interest = $2,000 × 0.05 = $100 per year.

entries.text: A fixed sum paid or received at equal intervals (for example every month) for a set number of periods, such as a loan repayment or a pension. The payment size is PMT = PV × r ÷ (1 − (1 + r)⁻ⁿ), where PV is the amount borrowed or the value today, r is the rate per period and n is the number of periods.
entries.example: A $10,000 loan at 1% a month over 12 months needs payments of about $888 a month.

entries.text: Paying off a debt in regular instalments, where each payment first covers the interest and the rest cuts the balance, so it reaches zero at the end. Early payments are mostly interest, and later payments are mostly principal.
entries.example: On a $1,000 balance at 1% a month, a $100 payment covers $10 of interest and reduces the balance to $910.

entries.text: A share of a company's profit paid to its shareholders, usually as cash for each share they own, often every quarter or year. Total dividend = dividend per share × number of shares owned.
entries.example: A company pays $0.50 per share; if you own 200 shares, you receive $0.50 × 200 = $100.

entries.text: The owners' stake in a business: what the business owns (its assets) minus what it owes (its liabilities), so Equity = assets − liabilities. In markets, people also use 'equity' to mean a company's shares of stock.
entries.example: A business with $50,000 of assets and $20,000 of debts has $30,000 of equity.

entries.text: A loan you give to a company or government, which pays you regular interest (the coupon) and repays the face value on a set end date called maturity.
entries.example: A $1,000 bond with a 4% coupon pays $40 a year and returns the $1,000 at maturity.

entries.text: The total of all future cash flows, each shrunk to today's money at a chosen rate r, minus the upfront cost. NPV = Σ CFₜ ÷ (1 + r)ᵗ − cost (summed over t = 1 to n), and a positive NPV means the project returns more than the rate r.
entries.example: Pay $1,000 now to get $1,100 in one year at r = 10%: NPV = 1,100 ÷ 1.10 − 1,000 = $0.

entries.text: The gain from an investment compared with what it cost, shown as a percentage. ROI = (money returned − cost) ÷ cost × 100%.
The share of sales revenue left after paying the direct cost of making or buying what was sold (cost of goods sold), shown as a percentage. Gross margin = (revenue − COGS) ÷ revenue × 100%.
entries.example: Sell an item for $40 that cost $25: gross margin = (40 − 25) ÷ 40 × 100% = 37.5%.

entries.text: A broad economic slowdown in which a country's output (GDP) shrinks for two or more quarters (three-month periods) in a row, a common rule of thumb. Spending, jobs and incomes usually fall during one.
entries.example: If GDP falls in both Q1 and Q2, the two-quarter rule calls that a recession.

entries.text: The total market value of all final goods and services made within a country in one period, usually a year or a quarter. GDP = C + I + G + (X − M), where C is consumer spending, I is investment, G is government spending, and X − M is net exports.
entries.example: Consumer spending $600bn + investment $200bn + government $150bn + net exports $50bn = GDP of $1,000bn.

entries.text: The value of the best alternative you give up when you make a choice, since you cannot have both. It counts what the money or time could have earned, not just what you paid.
entries.example: Spending $1,000 on a bike instead of leaving it in a savings account that earns $50 a year: the bike's opportunity cost includes that $50 of forgone interest.

entries.text: A sustained fall in the general level of prices, so the same money buys more over time; it is the opposite of inflation. Falling prices can make people delay spending, which can slow the economy.
entries.example: A basket of goods costing $100 one year and $97 the next has seen 3% deflation.

entries.text: Electric charge is a basic property of particles that makes them push or pull on each other; protons carry positive charge and electrons carry negative charge. Like charges repel, opposite charges attract, and charge is measured in coulombs (C).
entries.example: One electron has a charge of about −1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C.

entries.text: A coulomb (C) is the SI unit of electric charge: the amount of charge that flows past a point in one second when the current is one ampere (1 C = 1 A·s). That is about 6.24 × 10¹⁸ elementary charges, so it is a very large amount of charge.
entries.example: A current of 2 A flowing for 3 s moves 2 × 3 = 6 C of charge.

entries.text: An ampere (A) is the SI unit of electric current, equal to one coulomb of charge passing a point every second (1 A = 1 C/s). It measures how fast charge flows, the way litres per second measure how fast water flows.
entries.example: A device drawing 0.5 A moves 0.5 coulombs of charge every second.

entries.text: A watt (W) is the SI unit of power, meaning one joule of energy used or produced every second (1 W = 1 J/s). For electrical devices, power is voltage times current, P = V × I.
entries.example: A 60 W bulb on a 120 V supply draws 60 ÷ 120 = 0.5 A.

entries.text: A kilowatt-hour (kWh) is a unit of energy: the energy used by a 1-kilowatt device running for one hour. Electricity bills charge by the kWh, and one kWh equals 3.6 million joules (3.6 × 10⁶ J).
entries.example: A 100 W bulb left on for 10 hours uses 0.1 kW × 10 h = 1 kWh.

entries.text: A series circuit is a circuit where all components are connected end to end in one loop, so the same current flows through each one. The total resistance is the sum of the individual resistances, R = R₁ + R₂ + R₃, and if one component breaks the whole circuit stops.
entries.example: Three 10 Ω resistors in series give 10 + 10 + 10 = 30 Ω.

entries.text: A parallel circuit is a circuit where components are connected across the same two points, giving each branch its own path for the current. Every branch gets the full voltage, the branch currents add up to the total current, and if one branch breaks the others still work.
entries.example: Two 10 Ω resistors in parallel: 1/R = 1/10 + 1/10 = 2/10 = 1/5, so R = 5 Ω.

entries.text: A capacitor is a component that stores electric charge and energy between two conductive plates separated by an insulator. Its capacitance, measured in farads (F), is the charge stored divided by the voltage across it: capacitance = Q ÷ V.
entries.example: A 100 μF capacitor charged to 5 V stores 100 × 10⁻⁶ × 5 = 0.0005 C of charge.

entries.text: Alternating current (AC) is current that periodically reverses direction, switching back and forth many times each second. Household mains power completes 50 or 60 full back-and-forth cycles per second (50 Hz or 60 Hz, depending on the country), and transformers can easily step its voltage up or down.
entries.example: At 50 Hz the current reverses direction 100 times every second.

entries.text: Direct current (DC) is electric current that flows in only one direction, like the output of a battery or a USB charger. Its voltage and current stay roughly constant over time instead of swinging back and forth.
entries.example: A 9 V battery across a 3 Ω resistor drives a steady current of 9 ÷ 3 = 3 A.

entries.text: A short circuit is an unintended low-resistance connection that lets current skip past the normal load, such as when two bare wires touch. With almost no resistance to limit it, the current can become very large and overheat the wires, which is why fuses and circuit breakers are designed to cut the power fast.
entries.example: A 12 V supply across a 0.1 Ω short draws 12 ÷ 0.1 = 120 A, while a 12 Ω lamp draws only 1 A.

entries.text: A magnetic field is the invisible region around a magnet or a wire carrying current where magnetic forces act; outside a bar magnet it is drawn as field lines running from the north pole to the south pole. Its strength is measured in teslas (T).
entries.example: A compass needle lines up with Earth's magnetic field, which is about 50 μT (0.00005 T) at the surface.

entries.text: An electric field is the region around an electric charge where another charge would feel a push or pull. Its strength is the force per unit charge, E = F ÷ q, measured in newtons per coulomb (N/C).
entries.example: A 2 C charge that feels a 10 N force sits in a field of 10 ÷ 2 = 5 N/C.

entries.text: A farad (F) is the SI unit of capacitance: a capacitor has a capacitance of one farad if it stores one coulomb of charge when one volt is across it (1 F = 1 C/V). Real capacitors are usually rated in microfarads (μF) or picofarads (pF) because one farad is enormous.
entries.example: A 470 μF capacitor charged to 16 V stores 470 × 10⁻⁶ × 16 ≈ 0.0075 C.

entries.text: A tesla (T) is the SI unit of magnetic field strength, equal to one newton per ampere per metre (1 T = 1 N/(A·m)). Because it is a large unit, magnetic fields are often given in millitesla (mT) or microtesla (μT).
entries.example: An MRI scanner's 1.5 T field is 1.5 ÷ 0.00005 = 30,000 times stronger than Earth's field of about 50 μT.

entries.text: An atom is the smallest particle of an element that still has that element's identity. It has a dense nucleus of protons and usually neutrons, with electrons moving in the space around it.
entries.example: A carbon atom always has 6 protons, and that count is what makes it carbon.

entries.text: A molecule is a group of atoms held together by chemical bonds that acts as one particle. Water is a molecule of two hydrogen atoms and one oxygen atom, written H₂O.
entries.example: One molecule of H₂O contains 3 atoms in total: 2 hydrogen and 1 oxygen.

entries.text: An element is a substance made of only one kind of atom, meaning atoms that all have the same number of protons. There are 118 known elements, each with a symbol such as O for oxygen or Fe for iron.
entries.example: A gold ring is made only of gold (Au) atoms, so gold is an element.

entries.text: A compound is a substance made of two or more different elements chemically bonded in a fixed ratio. Its properties are usually very different from those of its elements: sodium chloride (NaCl) is table salt, made from a soft metal and a poisonous gas.
entries.example: H₂O is a compound because every molecule has 2 hydrogen atoms for every 1 oxygen atom, while O₂ is an element.

entries.text: An ion is an atom or group of atoms with an electric charge, caused by gaining or losing electrons. A positive ion has lost electrons, and a negative ion has gained them.
entries.example: Sodium loses one electron to form Na⁺, and chlorine gains one electron to form Cl⁻.

entries.text: Isotopes are atoms of the same element with different numbers of neutrons, so they have different mass numbers. They have the same number of protons, so they behave almost identically in chemical reactions.
entries.example: Carbon-14 has 6 protons and 8 neutrons, so its mass number is 6 + 8 = 14.

entries.text: The atomic number, written Z, is the number of protons in an atom's nucleus. It identifies the element: every atom with 8 protons is oxygen.
entries.example: Sodium has atomic number 11, so every sodium atom has 11 protons.

entries.text: Avogadro's number (Nₐ ≈ 6.022 × 10²³ per mole) is how many particles make up one mole of any substance. It links the tiny scale of atoms to amounts you can weigh in a lab.
entries.example: 12 g of carbon-12 contains about 6.022 × 10²³ carbon atoms, because 12 g is exactly one mole of it.

entries.text: Molarity is the number of moles of a dissolved substance (the solute) in each litre of solution, written M or mol/L. Formula: molarity = moles of solute ÷ litres of solution.
entries.example: Dissolving 0.5 mol of salt in enough water to make 2 L of solution gives 0.5 ÷ 2 = 0.25 M.

entries.text: Oxidation is the loss of electrons by an atom or ion during a reaction, and it always happens together with reduction, where another substance gains those electrons. The oxidation state (oxidation number) is a bookkeeping number that rises when an atom is oxidised.
entries.example: In 2Mg + O₂ → 2MgO, magnesium goes from oxidation state 0 to +2, so it is oxidised.

entries.text: A catalyst is a substance that speeds up a chemical reaction by giving it an easier pathway with a lower activation energy. It is not used up, so it is still there at the end of the reaction.
entries.example: Adding manganese dioxide (MnO₂) makes hydrogen peroxide decompose much faster, and the MnO₂ is still there afterwards.

entries.text: The periodic table is a chart of all known elements, arranged in order of increasing atomic number. Elements in the same column, called a group, tend to behave alike because they have the same number of outer electrons.
entries.example: Sodium (Na) and potassium (K) are both in Group 1, so both react vigorously with water.

entries.text: A covalent bond forms when two atoms share one or more pairs of electrons, holding both atoms together. It is the usual bond between non-metal atoms, as in H₂O and CH₄.
entries.example: In H₂, each hydrogen shares its one electron, forming one shared pair written H–H.

entries.text: An ionic bond is the electrical attraction between a positive ion and a negative ion, formed when one atom transfers electrons to another. It usually forms between a metal and a non-metal, such as sodium and chlorine in NaCl.
entries.example: Sodium gives one electron to chlorine: Na⁺ and Cl⁻ attract each other to form NaCl.

entries.text: Neutralisation is the reaction between an acid and a base, which produces a salt and water. The H⁺ ions from the acid and the OH⁻ ions from the base combine to form H₂O.
entries.example: HCl + NaOH → NaCl + H₂O: the H⁺ from HCl and the OH⁻ from NaOH combine into water, leaving the salt NaCl.

entries.text: The absolute value of a number is its distance from zero on the number line, so it is never negative: |x| = x if x ≥ 0, and |x| = −x if x < 0.
entries.example: |−7| = 7 and |7| = 7, because both are 7 steps away from zero.

entries.text: The reciprocal of a non-zero number x is 1 divided by x, written 1/x, and multiplying a number by its reciprocal always gives 1.
entries.example: The reciprocal of 4 is 1/4, because 4 × 1/4 = 1. Zero has no reciprocal since 1/0 is undefined.

entries.text: A coefficient is the number multiplied by a variable in a term; in 5x² the coefficient is 5, and a bare x has coefficient 1.
entries.example: In 3x + 7y − 2, the coefficients of x and y are 3 and 7, and the −2 is a constant.

entries.text: An inequality compares two expressions with one of the symbols < (less than), > (greater than), ≤ (less than or equal to), ≥ (greater than or equal to), or ≠ (not equal to), instead of saying they are equal.
entries.example: To solve 2x + 1 < 9: subtract 1 to get 2x < 8, then divide by 2 to get x < 4. Flip the sign if you multiply or divide by a negative number.

entries.text: A matrix is a rectangular grid of numbers arranged in rows and columns; one with m rows and n columns is called an m × n matrix.
entries.example: [[1, 2], [3, 4]] is a 2 × 2 matrix, and the entry in row 1, column 2 is 2.

entries.text: A vector is a quantity with both a size and a direction, written as a list of components such as (3, 4) for an arrow from the origin to that point.
entries.example: The length of the vector (3, 4) is √(3² + 4²) = √25 = 5.

entries.text: A set is a collection of distinct objects, written inside curly braces like A = {1, 2, 3}, where order does not matter and each item counts once.
entries.example: {1, 2, 2, 3} is the same set as {1, 2, 3}, because repeats are not counted twice.

entries.text: The domain of a function is the set of all input values (x-values) you are allowed to plug in to get a valid output; for example, you cannot divide by zero, so 1/x has every real number except 0 in its domain.
entries.example: f(x) = 1/(x − 2) has domain all real numbers except 2, since the denominator would be zero there.

entries.text: Exponential growth means a quantity is multiplied by the same factor b > 1 every equal time step, following y = a · bᵗ, where a is the starting amount and t is the number of steps.
entries.example: Starting with 100 users and doubling every hour gives y = 100 · 2ᵗ, so after 3 hours there are 100 · 2³ = 800 users.

entries.text: Exponential decay is the reverse: the quantity is multiplied by the same factor 0 < b < 1 every equal time step, following y = a · bᵗ.
entries.example: With a half-life of 5 years, after 10 years only (1/2)² = 1/4 of the original amount is left.

entries.text: The geometric mean of n positive numbers is the nth root of their product, ⁿ√(a₁ · a₂ · … · aₙ). It is the right average for growth factors, where values multiply rather than add.
entries.example: The geometric mean of 2 and 8 is √(2 · 8) = √16 = 4, while their arithmetic mean is 5.

entries.text: A scalar is a plain single number with a size but no direction, like a temperature of 20 °C or a mass of 5 kg. Multiplying a vector by a scalar stretches, shrinks, or (with a negative scalar) reverses it.
entries.example: Multiplying the vector (3, 4) by the scalar 2 gives (6, 8), which is twice as long and points the same way.

entries.text: A constant is a fixed value that never changes, such as the 7 in 3x + 7, or a fixed physical quantity like the speed of light c ≈ 3 × 10⁸ m/s.
entries.example: In y = 2x + 5, the 5 is a constant: it stays 5 no matter what x is.

entries.text: Set A is a subset of set B, written A ⊆ B, when every element of A is also an element of B.
entries.example: {1, 2} ⊆ {1, 2, 3} is true, but {1, 4} ⊆ {1, 2, 3} is false because 4 is not in the second set.

entries.text: Scientific notation writes a number as a × 10ⁿ, where 1 ≤ |a| < 10 and n is an integer, which makes very large or very small numbers easier to read.
entries.example: The speed of light, 300 000 000 m/s, becomes 3 × 10⁸ m/s.

entries.text: Displacement is how far an object ends up from where it started, measured in a straight line and including direction. It is the final position minus the starting position, Δx = x_final − x_initial, and it is measured in metres (m).
entries.example: A walker goes 5 m east and then 2 m west, so the displacement is 5 − 2 = 3 m east.

entries.text: Distance is the total length of the path an object travels, whichever way it goes. It is a scalar, so it has a size but no direction, it is never negative, and it is measured in metres (m).
entries.example: The same walker travels 5 m + 2 m, so the distance is 7 m even though the displacement is only 3 m.

entries.text: Work is the energy a force transfers to an object when the force moves the object along a distance. It is W = F·d·cos θ, where F is the force, d is the displacement and θ is the angle between them, and it is measured in joules (J), where 1 J = 1 N·m.
entries.example: Pushing a box with a 20 N force straight ahead for 3 m does W = 20 × 3 × cos 0° = 60 J.

entries.text: Friction is a force that opposes sliding, or attempted sliding, between two surfaces that touch. For sliding objects its size is f = μ·N, where μ is the coefficient of kinetic (sliding) friction (a number with no unit) and N is the normal force pressing the surfaces together, measured in newtons (N).
entries.example: A 10 kg box on a floor with μ = 0.3 has N = 10 × 9.8 = 98 N, so sliding friction is 0.3 × 98 ≈ 29 N.

entries.text: Gravity is the attractive pull between any two objects that have mass: the heavier they are, the stronger the pull, and the farther apart they are, the weaker it gets. The law of gravitation is F = G·m₁·m₂ / r², where G ≈ 6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ N·m²/kg², and near Earth's surface it gives falling objects an acceleration of g ≈ 9.8 m/s².
entries.example: Two 1 kg masses 1 m apart pull on each other with F = 6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ N, which is far too small to notice.

entries.text: Inertia is the tendency of an object to keep doing what it is already doing: a still object stays still, and a moving one keeps going in the same direction and at the same speed unless a net force changes it. The more mass an object has, the more inertia it has, so the harder it is to start, stop or turn.
entries.example: A bowling ball has much more inertia than a tennis ball, so it is much harder to start rolling or to stop once it is moving.

entries.text: Newton's three laws of motion describe how forces change motion. The first law says an object keeps its velocity unless a net force acts on it, the second says net force equals mass times acceleration (F = m·a), and the third says every action force has an equal and opposite reaction force acting on another object; the second law is the one used in most calculations.
entries.example: A 2 kg cart pushed by a net force of 10 N has acceleration a = F / m = 10 / 2 = 5 m/s².

entries.text: Frequency is how many complete cycles (waves or oscillations) happen each second. It is measured in hertz (Hz), where 1 Hz = 1 cycle per second, and it is the inverse of the period, f = 1 / T.
entries.example: A guitar string that vibrates 440 times each second has f = 440 Hz, so each vibration lasts T = 1 / 440 ≈ 0.00227 s.

entries.text: Wavelength is the distance from one point on a wave to the next identical point, such as crest to crest or trough to trough. It is measured in metres (m) and is linked to speed and frequency by v = f × λ.
entries.example: A wave with speed v = 340 m/s and frequency f = 170 Hz has λ = v / f = 340 / 170 = 2 m.

entries.text: Amplitude is the largest distance a wave or vibrating object moves away from its resting (middle) position. A bigger amplitude means a louder sound or a brighter light, and it has the same unit as displacement, such as metres (m).
entries.example: A string pulled 3 cm away from rest and then released has amplitude 3 cm, so its full swing from one side to the other is 6 cm.

entries.text: Centripetal force is the net inward force that keeps an object moving in a circle, always pointing toward the centre of that circle. It is not a new kind of force: it is whatever real force, such as string tension or gravity, points toward the centre, and its size is F = m·v² / r, where m is mass, v is speed and r is the radius, measured in newtons (N).
entries.example: A 0.5 kg ball on a 1 m string moving at 4 m/s needs F = 0.5 × 4² / 1 = 8 N toward the centre.

entries.text: Torque is the turning effect a force has on an object around a pivot, and it is bigger when the force is larger, applied farther from the pivot, or pushing at a right angle. It is τ = r·F·sin θ, where r is the distance from the pivot, F is the force and θ is the angle between r and F, measured in newton-metres (N·m).
entries.example: Pushing a door 0.8 m from its hinge with 50 N at a right angle gives τ = 0.8 × 50 × sin 90° = 40 N·m.

entries.text: Efficiency is the share of the energy or work you put into a machine that comes out as useful output, with the rest usually lost as heat or sound. It is efficiency = (useful output ÷ total input) × 100%, so it is always between 0% and 100%.
entries.example: A motor that takes in 200 J and delivers 150 J of useful work has efficiency = 150 ÷ 200 × 100% = 75%.

entries.text: The period is the time taken for one complete cycle of a wave or repeating motion, such as one full back-and-forth swing of a pendulum. It is measured in seconds (s) and is the inverse of frequency, T = 1 / f.
entries.example: A pendulum that completes 4 full back-and-forth cycles in 8 s has T = 8 / 4 = 2 s per cycle, so its frequency is f = 1 / 2 = 0.5 Hz.

entries.text: A wave is a disturbance that carries energy from one place to another without carrying the material it moves through along with it. Waves are described by amplitude, wavelength, frequency and speed (linked by v = f × λ), and they are either transverse, where particles move at right angles to the direction of travel like ripples on a rope, or longitudinal, where particles move along the direction of travel like sound in air.
entries.example: A ripple spreading across a pond carries energy outward, but a leaf on the water only bobs up and down in place.

entries.text: An algorithm is a finite, step-by-step set of instructions that turns an input into a desired output. Sorting a list, finding the shortest route on a map, and a recipe for bread are all algorithms.
entries.example: To find the biggest number in a list, keep the largest value seen so far and compare each new item against it.

entries.text: A byte is a unit of digital information made of 8 bits, so it can hold 256 different values (0 to 255). Storage is counted in bytes, with 1 KB = 1,000 bytes and 1 MB = 1,000,000 bytes in decimal units.
entries.example: In the common ASCII code the letter 'A' is stored as the byte 65, so the word 'CAT' takes 3 bytes.

entries.text: A bit (short for binary digit) is the smallest unit of digital information and holds just one value, 0 or 1. A group of n bits can represent 2ⁿ different values, so 8 bits give 2⁸ = 256 values.

An API (application programming interface) is a defined set of rules that lets one program request data or actions from another in a predictable way. It works like a restaurant menu: you choose from the listed options and never need to see how the kitchen cooks.
entries.example: A weather app asks a weather service's API for the temperature in London right now and gets back a structured answer it can display.

entries.text: A database is an organized collection of data stored so it can be searched, added to, changed and kept reliable over time. Software that manages a database, such as PostgreSQL or MySQL, is called a database management system (DBMS).
entries.example: A shop's customers table has one row per customer, with columns for name, email and signup date.

entries.text: A cache is a small, fast store that keeps copies of data that are slow to fetch, so repeat requests can be answered quickly. A cache hit means the item was already stored, while a cache miss means it was not and the slow original source must be used.
entries.example: A product price cached for 60 seconds lets the first visitor trigger one database query, while the next 99 visitors in that minute get the saved copy.

entries.text: Throughput is how much work a system finishes per unit of time: throughput = completed items ÷ time taken, such as requests per second (RPS). Latency measures how long one request takes, while throughput measures how many requests finish overall.
entries.example: A server that completes 600 requests in 60 seconds has a throughput of 600 ÷ 60 = 10 requests per second.

entries.text: Big O notation describes how the number of steps an algorithm needs grows as its input size n grows, ignoring constant factors and small details. O(n) means the work grows in step with n, while O(n²) means doubling the input roughly quadruples the work.
entries.example: Checking every name in a list of 1,000 takes about 1,000 steps, O(n), while binary search on a sorted list takes about 10 steps, O(log n), since 2¹⁰ = 1,024.

entries.text: Recursion is when a function solves a problem by calling itself on a smaller version of the same problem. Every recursive function needs a base case, a simple version it can answer directly, so the calls eventually stop.
entries.example: Using n! = n × (n−1)! with base case 1! = 1, the function computes 4! as 4 × 3 × 2 × 1 = 24 by calling itself on smaller numbers each time.

entries.text: A hash function turns any input, like a password or a file, into a fixed-length code called a hash, and the same input always gives the same hash. Cryptographic hash functions are designed to be one-way, so the original input is practically impossible to recover from the hash, and even a tiny change to the input gives a completely different hash.
entries.example: The SHA-256 hash of anything, from one letter to a whole movie, is always 256 bits, written as 64 hex characters.

entries.text: Encryption scrambles data with a mathematical method and a secret key, so only someone holding the right key can turn it back into readable form. Unlike hashing, encryption is reversible, because decrypting with the key recovers the original data.
entries.example: Shifting each letter of 'HI' forward by 3 gives 'KL' (a Caesar cipher), and the receiver shifts each letter back by 3 to read 'HI' again.

entries.text: Bandwidth is the maximum amount of data a network connection can carry each second, measured in bits per second (bps), such as megabits per second (Mbps). It describes the capacity of the connection, not how fast any single piece of data travels.
entries.example: A 100 Mbps connection can carry at most 100 ÷ 8 = 12.5 megabytes of data each second.

entries.text: Uptime is the share of time a service is running and able to respond, usually written as a percentage: uptime % = (time up ÷ total time) × 100. For example, 99.9% uptime allows about 8.8 hours of downtime in a year.
entries.example: A service that is down for 2 hours in a 30-day month (720 hours) has uptime of (718 ÷ 720) × 100 ≈ 99.72%.

entries.text: A rate limit caps how many requests a client can make in a set time window, such as 100 per minute, so one user or bot cannot overload a service. Requests over the limit are usually refused with HTTP status 429 (Too Many Requests).
entries.example: An API allowing 100 requests per minute rejects the 101st request in the same minute with a 429 error.

entries.text: An array is an ordered collection of values usually stored one after another in memory, each reached by its index (its position number). Most programming languages start indexes at 0, so the first item is at index 0.
entries.example: The array ['red', 'green', 'blue'] has length 3, and the item at index 1 is 'green'.

entries.text: A sample is a smaller group that you actually measure, often chosen at random, so you can learn about a bigger group without checking every member. The number of items in it is the sample size, written n.
entries.example: Asking 50 of a school's 800 students whether they like pizza: the 50 students are the sample, so n = 50.

entries.text: A population is the entire group you want to know something about, such as every customer a shop has ever had. Its size is written N, and a number that describes the whole population, like its true average, is called a parameter.
entries.example: All 800 students in a school form the population (N = 800), and their true average height is a population parameter.

entries.text: A hypothesis test checks whether data give real evidence against a default claim, called the null hypothesis. It compares what you observed with what pure chance would usually produce, and if your result would be very unlikely under the default claim, you reject that claim.
entries.example: Getting 9 heads in 10 flips of a coin: the test asks whether a fair coin could easily do that by luck, or whether the coin is probably biased.

entries.text: The null hypothesis (H₀) is the default claim that nothing interesting is going on, such as 'this coin is fair' or 'the new layout changes nothing'. A hypothesis test checks whether the data are too unusual for that claim to be true.
entries.example: H₀: the coin is fair, so P(heads) = 0.5.

entries.text: A p-value is the chance of getting a result at least as extreme as yours if the null hypothesis were true. A small p-value (often below 0.05) means the data would be surprising under that claim, so it counts as evidence against it.
entries.example: 9 or more heads in 10 fair flips has probability 11/1024 ≈ 0.011, so the one-sided p-value is about 0.011.

entries.text: A confidence interval is a range built from sample data that is designed to contain the true population value, such as the true average. A 95% confidence interval means the method would capture the true value in about 95 out of 100 repeated samples.
entries.example: A poll of 1,000 people finds 52% support, with a 95% confidence interval of roughly 49% to 55%.

entries.text: The normal distribution is a symmetric bell-shaped pattern where most values sit near the mean and fewer sit farther away. It is set by the mean μ and standard deviation σ, and about 68% of values fall within 1σ of the mean while about 95% fall within 2σ.
entries.example: Adult heights are roughly normal with mean 170 cm and σ = 10 cm, so about 68% of adults are between 160 cm and 180 cm.

entries.text: The binomial distribution gives the chance of exactly k successes in n independent yes-or-no tries, where each try succeeds with chance p. The formula is P(k) = C(n,k) · pᵏ · (1 − p)ⁿ⁻ᵏ, where C(n,k) counts the ways to choose which tries are successes.
entries.example: Flipping a fair coin 3 times, P(exactly 2 heads) = 3 × 0.5² × 0.5 = 0.375.

entries.text: The expected value is the long-run average of a random outcome: multiply each possible value by its probability and add the results. Written E(X) = Σ xᵢ · P(xᵢ), it is what the average gets close to after many repeats, even if you can never get exactly that value.
entries.example: A game pays $10 with probability 0.2 and $0 otherwise, so E = 10 × 0.2 + 0 × 0.8 = $2.

entries.text: Two events are independent when one happening does not change the chance of the other, so P(A and B) = P(A) × P(B). Two coin flips are independent, but drawing two cards from a deck without putting the first back is not, because the first draw changes what is left.
entries.example: For two fair coin flips, P(heads then heads) = 0.5 × 0.5 = 0.25.

entries.text: Regression finds the straight line that best predicts one value from another, usually by making the squared vertical gaps between the points and the line as small as possible. The line is written ŷ = a + b·x, where the slope b says how much y changes for each extra 1 of x.
entries.example: If predicted test score ŷ = 40 + 6x for x hours of study, then 5 hours predicts 40 + 6 × 5 = 70 points.

entries.text: The interquartile range (IQR) is the width of the middle half of sorted data: Q3 − Q1, the 75th percentile minus the 25th percentile. Because it ignores the lowest and highest quarters, a few extreme outliers barely change it.
entries.example: For 2, 4, 6, 8, 10, 12, 14, 16, splitting into halves gives Q1 = 5 (median of 2, 4, 6, 8) and Q3 = 13 (median of 10, 12, 14, 16), so IQR = 13 − 5 = 8.

entries.text: Quartiles are three cut-points that split sorted data into four equal-sized parts. Q1 is the lower quartile (about the 25th percentile), Q2 is the median (50th percentile), and Q3 is the upper quartile (about the 75th percentile).
entries.example: For the numbers 1 to 8, splitting them into halves 1 to 4 and 5 to 8 gives Q1 = 2.5, Q2 = 4.5, Q3 = 6.5.

entries.text: Conditional probability is the chance of event A once you already know event B happened, written P(A | B) and read 'probability of A given B'. It equals P(A and B) ÷ P(B), because you shrink the possibilities down to only the cases where B is true.
entries.example: A 52-card deck has 12 face cards, 4 of which are kings, so P(king | face card) = 4 ÷ 12 = 1/3.

entries.text: A random variable is a quantity whose value depends on chance, such as the number rolled on a die or the number of heads in 3 coin flips. Each possible value, or range of values, has a probability, and together these form its probability distribution.
entries.example: Let X be the number of heads in 3 fair flips: X takes the values 0, 1, 2, 3 with probabilities 1/8, 3/8, 3/8, 1/8.

entries.text: Downtime is the time a service is unavailable or broken for its users, usually counted in minutes or hours. Downtime % = 100% − uptime %, so it is simply the other side of uptime.
entries.example: A site down for 90 minutes in a 30-day month (43,200 minutes) has downtime 90 ÷ 43,200 ≈ 0.21%.

entries.text: An SLA (service level agreement) is a formal contract with customers that promises a service level, such as 99.9% uptime. If the promise is broken, the provider owes something, usually service credits or refunds.
entries.example: A contract promises 99.9% monthly uptime with a 10% credit if missed; a month at 99.5% triggers the credit.

entries.text: An SLO (service level objective) is an internal target for an SLI, such as 'at least 99.9% of requests succeed over 30 days'. It is usually set tighter than the SLA so the team is warned before customers are hurt.
entries.example: Target: 99.9% of requests succeed over 30 days. Actual: 99.95%, so the SLO is met.

entries.text: An SLI (service level indicator) is a measurement of how well a service is doing, written as a ratio: SLI = good events ÷ total events. Common examples are the share of requests that succeed or the share that finish under 300 ms.
entries.example: 1,998,000 successful requests out of 2,000,000 gives SLI = 1,998,000 ÷ 2,000,000 = 99.9%.

entries.text: An error budget is how much unreliability an SLO allows: error budget = 1 − SLO, so a 99.9% SLO leaves 0.1% of events allowed to fail. Teams spend the budget on risky releases and slow down when it runs out.
entries.example: With a 99.9% SLO over 30 days, the budget is 0.1% × 43,200 minutes ≈ 43 minutes of allowed downtime.

entries.text: Burn rate is how fast the error budget is being used compared with the pace that would use it up exactly at the end of the SLO window: burn rate = observed error rate ÷ (1 − SLO). A burn rate of 1 lasts the full window, and 10 empties it in one tenth of the time.
entries.example: With a 99.9% SLO, a 1% error rate gives burn rate 0.01 ÷ 0.001 = 10, so a 30-day budget is gone in 3 days.

entries.text: Alert fatigue is when people receive so many alerts, many of them false or unimportant, that they start ignoring them or respond slowly, so real problems get missed. The fix is usually fewer, more meaningful alerts where each one needs action.
entries.example: A team paged 200 times a week, mostly for noise, may miss the one page that signals a real outage.

entries.text: MTTR (mean time to recovery, sometimes repair or resolve) is the average time from when a failure starts or is detected until service is working again: MTTR = total recovery time ÷ number of incidents. Lower MTTR means problems are fixed faster.
entries.example: Three outages lasting 20, 40 and 30 minutes give MTTR = (20 + 40 + 30) ÷ 3 = 30 minutes.

entries.text: On-call is a duty in which an engineer must be reachable and ready to respond to alerts for a set period, often a week, including outside working hours. Teams rotate the duty so the load is shared.
entries.example: Priya is on-call for one week, so a checkout failure at 3 a.m. pages her phone.

entries.text: A runbook is a written step-by-step guide that tells an on-call person how to check, diagnose and fix a known problem. Good runbooks let someone who has never seen the failure still act on the alert.
entries.example: Alert: checkout errors above 5%. Step 1: check the payment provider's status page. Step 2: roll back the last deploy.

entries.text: A postmortem is a written review made after an incident is resolved, covering what happened, the impact, the root causes and the follow-up actions. Good postmortems are blameless, asking how the system and process allowed the failure rather than who made a mistake.
entries.example: After a 45-minute outage from a bad config push, the postmortem adds a config check so the same push cannot ship again.

entries.text: A false negative is when a detector stays silent even though a real problem is happening, such as a metric crashing with no alert firing. Its rate = real problems missed ÷ all real problems, and lowering it usually raises false positives, so the two trade off.
entries.example: Ten real outages happen and the alert fires for only seven: 3 false negatives, a 30% miss rate.

entries.text: A tangent line is the straight line that touches a curve at a point and has the same steepness as the curve right there. If y = f(x), the tangent at x = a has slope f′(a) and equation y − f(a) = f′(a)(x − a).
entries.example: For y = x² at x = 3, the slope is f′(3) = 6, so the tangent line is y = 6x − 9.

entries.text: A secant line is a straight line that cuts through two points on a curve. Its slope, (f(b) − f(a)) ÷ (b − a), is the average rate of change of the function between x = a and x = b.
entries.example: For y = x² from x = 1 to x = 3, the secant slope is (9 − 1) ÷ (3 − 1) = 4.

entries.text: The chain rule gives the derivative of a function nested inside another function, like f(g(x)). Take the derivative of the outer function, leave the inside alone, and multiply by the derivative of the inside: d/dx f(g(x)) = f′(g(x)) · g′(x).
entries.example: For (3x + 1)⁵, the derivative is 5(3x + 1)⁴ · 3 = 15(3x + 1)⁴.

entries.text: The product rule gives the derivative of two functions multiplied together: take the derivative of the first times the second, plus the first times the derivative of the second. Formula: (f · g)′ = f′ · g + f · g′.
entries.example: For x² · sin x, the derivative is 2x · sin x + x² · cos x.

entries.text: The quotient rule gives the derivative of one function divided by another. Formula: (f ÷ g)′ = (f′ · g − f · g′) ÷ g², meaning (bottom × derivative of top − top × derivative of bottom) ÷ bottom².
entries.example: For x ÷ (x + 1), the derivative is ((1)(x + 1) − x(1)) ÷ (x + 1)² = 1 ÷ (x + 1)².

entries.text: A definite integral, written ∫ from a to b of f(x) dx, gives the exact signed area between the curve y = f(x) and the x-axis from x = a to x = b. Area above the x-axis counts as positive and area below it counts as negative.
entries.example: ∫ from 0 to 2 of x dx = 2, because the triangle under y = x from 0 to 2 has area ½ · 2 · 2 = 2.

entries.text: A function is continuous at a point if its graph has no gap, jump or hole there, so you could draw through that point without lifting your pencil. Formally, the limit as x → a of f(x) must exist and equal f(a).
entries.example: f(x) = x² is continuous at x = 2, since the limit as x → 2 of x² is 4 = f(2).

entries.text: An asymptote is a line that a curve keeps getting closer to, usually as x or y runs off toward infinity or near a point where the curve blows up. A vertical asymptote x = a means f(x) shoots toward ±∞ as x nears a, and a horizontal asymptote y = L means f(x) → L as x → ±∞.
entries.example: f(x) = 1/x has a vertical asymptote at x = 0 and a horizontal asymptote at y = 0.

entries.text: A local maximum is a peak: a point where the function's value is at least as large as at every nearby point, even if the function is higher somewhere far away. For a smooth curve, the slope is zero there (f′(x) = 0), and the graph switches from rising to falling.
entries.example: f(x) = −x² + 4 has a local maximum at x = 0, where f′(0) = 0 and f(0) = 4.

entries.text: A local minimum is a valley: a point where the function's value is no larger than at every nearby point, even if the function is lower somewhere far away. For a smooth curve, the slope is zero there (f′(x) = 0), and the graph switches from falling to rising.
entries.example: f(x) = x² − 6x + 10 has a local minimum at x = 3, where f(3) = 1 and f′(3) = 0.

entries.text: An inflection point is where a curve changes the way it bends, switching from curving up (like a cup) to curving down (like a frown) or the other way around. It occurs where the second derivative f″(x) changes sign.
entries.example: f(x) = x³ has an inflection point at x = 0, because f″(x) = 6x changes from negative to positive there.

entries.text: A differential equation is an equation that links an unknown function with its derivatives, so it describes how something changes. For example, dy/dt = ky says the rate of change of y is proportional to y, and its solution is y(t) = y₀ · e^(kt), where y₀ is the value of y at t = 0.
entries.example: dy/dt = 2y with y(0) = 5 has the solution y(t) = 5e^(2t), since its derivative 10e^(2t) equals 2 · 5e^(2t).

entries.text: A sequence converges when its terms settle toward one specific finite number as you go further along, and a series converges when its running totals (partial sums) do; that number is the limit or sum. If they do not settle down, for example by growing forever or bouncing around, they diverge.
entries.example: The series 1 + ½ + ¼ + ⅛ + ... converges to 2, because its partial sums get ever closer to 2.

entries.text: The fundamental theorem of calculus says that integration and differentiation undo each other. In practice, the definite integral of f from a to b equals F(b) − F(a), where F is any antiderivative of f, so you can find areas without adding up tiny slices.
entries.example: ∫ from 1 to 3 of 2x dx = [x²] from 1 to 3 = 9 − 1 = 8.

entries.text: The odds of an event are the chance it happens compared with the chance it doesn't. If the probability is p, the odds are p / (1 − p). Odds of 3 to 1 mean it is three times as likely to happen as not.
entries.example: A 75% chance of rain means odds of 0.75 / 0.25 = 3 to 1.

entries.text: Bayes' theorem is a formula for flipping a conditional probability: P(A|B) = P(B|A) · P(A) / P(B). It lets you update how likely something is after you see new evidence.
entries.example: A test that is 99% sensitive and 99% specific, for a disease with 1 case in 1,000 people, gives a positive result that means truly sick only about 9% of the time.

entries.text: The sample space is the set of all possible outcomes of a random experiment, often written S or Ω. An event is any subset of the sample space.
entries.example: For one roll of a die, S = {1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6}; for two coin flips, S = {HH, HT, TH, TT}.

entries.text: Covariance measures whether two variables tend to move together: it is positive when they rise together and negative when one rises as the other falls. For a sample it is cov(X, Y) = Σ(xᵢ − x̄)(yᵢ − ȳ) / (n − 1), and its units are the product of the two variables' units.
entries.example: Hours studied and exam scores usually have positive covariance.

entries.text: Regression to the mean is the tendency for an extreme measurement to be followed by one closer to the average. Extreme results are partly due to luck, and luck does not repeat reliably.
entries.example: A student who scores unusually high on one quiz usually scores closer to their average on the next quiz.

entries.text: The central limit theorem says that the average of many independent random values is approximately normally distributed (bell-shaped), no matter what the original distribution looks like (as long as its variance is finite), once the sample is large enough. The spread of that average shrinks as σ / √n.
entries.example: A single die roll is flat across 1 to 6, but the average of 30 rolls clusters in a bell shape around 3.5.

entries.text: A type I error happens when you reject the null hypothesis even though it is true, which is a false alarm. Its probability is called alpha (α), the significance level of the test.
entries.example: Concluding that a useless drug works when it actually does nothing is a type I error.

entries.text: The standard error is the standard deviation of a sample statistic, usually the sample mean, across many repeated samples. For a mean it is SE = s / √n, and it shows how precisely the sample estimates the true population value.
entries.example: With a standard deviation of 15 and a sample of 100 people, SE = 15 / √100 = 1.5.

entries.text: Skewness measures how lopsided a distribution is. Positive skew means a long tail to the right (the mean is pulled above the median), negative skew means a long tail to the left, and a symmetric distribution has skewness 0.
entries.example: Household incomes are usually positively skewed, because a few very high incomes stretch the right tail.

entries.text: The harmonic mean is n divided by the sum of the reciprocals of n values: H = n / (1/x₁ + … + 1/xₙ). It is the right average for rates measured over equal amounts of the other quantity, such as speeds over equal distances.
entries.example: Driving 60 km/h one way and 40 km/h back over the same distance averages 2 / (1/60 + 1/40) = 48 km/h, not 50.

entries.text: A weighted average gives each value a weight showing how much it counts, computed as Σwᵢxᵢ / Σwᵢ. When all weights are equal, it is the ordinary mean.
entries.example: A course with a 30% homework grade of 80 and a 70% exam grade of 90 has a weighted average of 0.3 × 80 + 0.7 × 90 = 87.

entries.text: The margin of error is how far a sample estimate can plausibly be from the true value, usually written as ± and calculated as about z × SE at a chosen confidence level. Smaller samples and more variable data make it larger.
entries.example: A poll of 1,000 people showing 52% support has a 95% margin of error of about ±3 percentage points.

entries.text: A single number computed from a square matrix that shows how much the matrix scales area or volume. For a 2×2 matrix it equals ad − bc, and if it is 0 the matrix squashes space flat and has no inverse.
A number λ such that a square matrix A only stretches a special vector v by λ, so Av = λv. You find eigenvalues by solving det(A − λI) = 0.
entries.example: For A = [[2,0],[0,3]], the eigenvalues are 2 and 3.

entries.text: A nonzero vector v that keeps its direction when a matrix A acts on it, so Av = λv and only its length changes, by the factor λ.
entries.example: For A = [[2,0],[0,3]], the vector (1, 0) is an eigenvector with eigenvalue 2.

entries.text: A square matrix with 1s down the main diagonal and 0s everywhere else. Multiplying any matrix by it leaves that matrix unchanged, just as multiplying a number by 1 does: AI = IA = A.
entries.example: The 2×2 identity matrix is [[1,0],[0,1]].

entries.text: The matrix Aᵀ made by flipping A over its main diagonal, so rows become columns and columns become rows. The entry in row i, column j moves to row j, column i.

Multiplies two vectors of the same length and gives a single number: a·b = a₁b₁ + a₂b₂ + … + aₙbₙ, which also equals |a||b|cos θ. The result is positive when the vectors point roughly the same way and zero when they are perpendicular.
Multiplies two 3D vectors to give a new 3D vector perpendicular to both, with length |a||b|sin θ. That length equals the area of the parallelogram the two vectors span.
Arithmetic where numbers wrap around after a fixed value called the modulus n, like hours on a clock. a mod n is the remainder when a is divided by n.
a ≡ b (mod n) means a and b leave the same remainder when divided by n, which is the same as saying n divides a − b.
The set of everything that is in set A, in set B, or in both. It is written A ∪ B and repeated elements are listed only once.
The set of elements that are in both set A and set B, written A ∩ B. If the two sets share nothing, the intersection is the empty set ∅.

A collection of dots, called vertices or nodes, joined by lines, called edges, that show which pairs are connected. Graphs model things like road maps, social networks and the internet, and they are not the same as charts of data.
entries.example: Four cities with roads joining some pairs of them form a graph.

entries.text: A connected graph with no cycles, meaning no route that loops back to where it started. A tree with n vertices always has exactly n − 1 edges, and one vertex is often chosen as the root.
entries.example: A family tree or a folder structure on a computer is a tree.

entries.text: To prove a statement P, assume P is false and show this leads to something impossible, such as a statement that contradicts itself. Since the assumption causes a contradiction, P must be true.
entries.example: To prove √2 is irrational, assume √2 = p/q in lowest terms; then p and q are both even, which contradicts being in lowest terms.

entries.text: A way to prove a statement holds for every whole number n ≥ 1: first check the base case n = 1, then show that if it holds for n = k it also holds for n = k + 1. These two steps knock down a chain of dominoes covering every case.
entries.example: To prove 1 + 2 + … + n = n(n + 1)/2, check n = 1 gives 1 = 1, then assume it for k and add k + 1 to both sides.

entries.text: Shortcuts for working with logarithms, for positive numbers x and y: log(xy) = log x + log y, log(x/y) = log x − log y, log(xᵏ) = k·log x, and log_b x = (log x)/(log b) for any base b. They turn multiplication into addition, which is why logarithms were once used for calculation.
entries.example: log₂(8 · 4) = log₂8 + log₂4 = 3 + 2 = 5.

entries.text: A compact way to write a sum using the Greek capital letter Σ (sigma). The index below Σ gives the starting value, the number above gives the ending value, and the expression to the right is added for each value: Σ from i = 1 to n of aᵢ means a₁ + a₂ + … + aₙ.
entries.example: Σ from i = 1 to 4 of i² = 1 + 4 + 9 + 16 = 30.

entries.text: Temperature measures how hot or cold something is, and it reflects the average kinetic energy of its particles. It is measured in kelvin (K), degrees Celsius (°C), or degrees Fahrenheit (°F).
entries.example: Water freezes at 273.15 K, which is 0 °C.

entries.text: Heat is energy that flows from a hotter object to a cooler one because of a temperature difference. It is measured in joules (J).
entries.example: A hot pan warms the cold water inside it until they reach the same temperature.

entries.text: Specific heat capacity is the energy needed to raise the temperature of 1 kg of a substance by 1 K (or 1 °C). It is calculated as c = Q / (m · ΔT) and measured in J/(kg·K).
entries.example: Water has a specific heat capacity of about 4186 J/(kg·K), so it takes a lot of energy to heat it.

entries.text: Entropy is a measure of how spread out or disordered energy and matter are in a system. In an isolated system it tends to increase, and it is measured in J/K.
entries.example: When ice melts, its molecules move into a less ordered state, so the entropy increases.

entries.text: Thermal equilibrium is the state in which objects in contact have the same temperature, so no net heat flows between them. It is the endpoint of heat transfer.
entries.example: A cup of coffee left in a room eventually reaches thermal equilibrium with the room's air.

entries.text: Refraction is the bending of a wave, such as light, when it passes from one material into another where its speed changes. The amount of bending is given by Snell's law: n₁ · sin θ₁ = n₂ · sin θ₂.
entries.example: A straw in a glass of water looks bent at the surface because light refracts as it leaves the water.

entries.text: Reflection is the bouncing back of a wave off a surface. For light bouncing off a smooth surface, the angle of incidence equals the angle of reflection.
entries.example: A mirror shows your image because light reflects off its smooth surface.

entries.text: The speed of light is the speed at which light travels through a vacuum, exactly 299,792,458 m/s, or about 3 × 10⁸ m/s. Nothing with mass can reach this speed.
entries.example: Sunlight takes about 8 minutes to travel from the Sun to Earth.

entries.text: A photon is a particle of light, the smallest unit of light or other electromagnetic radiation. Its energy is E = h · f, where h is Planck's constant and f is the frequency.
entries.example: Each photon that leaves your phone screen carries a tiny amount of energy that depends only on its color (frequency).

entries.text: Half-life is the time it takes for half of the radioactive nuclei in a sample to decay. It is a fixed property of each radioactive isotope.
entries.example: Carbon-14 has a half-life of about 5,730 years, so half of it is gone after that time.

entries.text: Radioactivity is the spontaneous release of radiation, such as alpha, beta, or gamma rays, from unstable atomic nuclei as they change into more stable forms. Activity is measured in becquerels (Bq), where 1 Bq equals one decay per second.
entries.example: Uranium in rocks gives off radiation as its nuclei decay over time.

entries.text: Escape velocity is the minimum speed an object needs at a planet's surface to break free of its gravity without any further thrust. It is calculated as v = √(2GM / r).
entries.example: Earth's escape velocity is about 11.2 km/s.

entries.text: A gravitational field is the region around a mass where another mass feels an attractive force. Its strength is g = F / m, measured in N/kg, which is the same as m/s².
entries.example: Near Earth's surface the gravitational field strength is about 9.8 N/kg.

entries.text: Buoyancy is the upward push a fluid exerts on any object placed in it. This push makes objects feel lighter when they are in water.
entries.example: A wooden boat floats because the water pushes it upward with a force equal to its weight.

entries.text: Archimedes' principle states that an object in a fluid feels an upward buoyant force equal to the weight of the fluid it displaces. It is written as F_b = ρ_fluid · V · g, where V is the displaced volume.
entries.example: A steel ship floats because its hull pushes aside enough water to weigh as much as the ship.

entries.text: The friction coefficient (μ) is a unitless number that describes how grippy two surfaces are against each other. The friction force is F = μ · N, where N is the normal force pressing the surfaces together.
entries.example: Rubber tires on dry asphalt have a friction coefficient of roughly 0.7 to 0.9.

entries.text: A cell is the smallest unit of life: a tiny, membrane-wrapped bubble of chemistry that can take in food, make energy, and copy itself. Every plant, animal, and human is built from one or more cells.
entries.example: Your skin, muscle, and blood are made of trillions of cells, and a single bacterium is one cell.

entries.text: DNA is a long, twisted molecule (a double helix) that stores the instructions for building and running a living thing. It is made of four chemical letters, A, T, C, and G, arranged in a specific order.
entries.example: Humans have about 3 billion DNA letters in each cell, split into 46 chromosomes.

entries.text: A gene is a segment of DNA that carries the instructions for making one specific protein or functional molecule. Genes are passed from parents to children and help determine traits such as eye color.
entries.example: A gene for blue eyes and a gene for brown eyes are two possible versions of the same eye-color gene.

entries.text: A protein is a large molecule built from a chain of smaller units called amino acids, folded into a specific 3D shape that lets it do a job. Proteins make up muscles, carry oxygen, and act as the body's messengers and tools.
entries.example: Hemoglobin is a protein in red blood cells that carries oxygen from your lungs to the rest of your body.

entries.text: An enzyme is a protein that speeds up a chemical reaction in a living thing without being used up itself. Each enzyme usually works on only one kind of molecule, like a key that fits one lock.
entries.example: Amylase is an enzyme in your saliva that starts breaking down starch in bread into sugar.

entries.text: A virus is a tiny infectious particle made of genetic material (DNA or RNA) inside a protein coat. It cannot grow or reproduce on its own and must invade a host cell to make copies of itself.
entries.example: Influenza and the common cold are caused by viruses, which is why antibiotics do not cure them.

entries.text: Bacteria are single-celled living organisms that are much simpler than plant or animal cells and can reproduce on their own. Most bacteria are harmless or helpful, such as those in your gut, while some cause infections.
entries.example: Escherichia coli lives in the human gut, and Streptococcus can cause strep throat.

entries.text: A vaccine is a substance that trains the immune system to recognize a germ, using a harmless piece of it or a weakened or inactivated version, so the body can fight the real infection faster later. Vaccines prevent disease without usually causing the illness itself.
entries.example: The measles vaccine teaches the body to make antibodies so a later measles infection is stopped early.

entries.text: An antibody is a Y-shaped protein made by the immune system that attaches to a specific germ or toxin and marks it for destruction. Each antibody is shaped to match one particular target, like a custom lock for one key.
entries.example: After you recover from chickenpox, antibodies stay in your blood and help protect you from getting it again.

entries.text: Metabolism is the total of all chemical reactions in a living thing that break down food to release energy and build up the molecules the body needs. The basal metabolic rate is the energy a person burns at complete rest just to keep vital functions running.
entries.example: Your liver, brain, and muscles all use metabolism to turn food into the energy that powers your heartbeat and movement.

entries.text: A calorie is a unit of energy, the amount needed to raise 1 gram of water by 1 °C. On food labels, the word calorie really means a kilocalorie (kcal), which is 1,000 of those small calories, or about 4,184 joules.
entries.example: A medium apple has about 95 kcal, which is the energy your body can get from eating it.

entries.text: Body mass index (BMI) is a rough number that compares a person's weight to their height, calculated as BMI = weight (kg) ÷ height (m)². It is a quick screening tool and does not measure body fat or fitness directly.
entries.example: A person who weighs 70 kg and is 1.75 m tall has a BMI of 70 ÷ (1.75 × 1.75) ≈ 22.9.

entries.text: Resting heart rate is the number of times your heart beats per minute while you are calm and inactive, usually measured after waking up. For most adults, a normal range is about 60 to 100 beats per minute, and well-trained athletes often have lower numbers.
entries.example: If you count 72 beats in one minute while sitting quietly, your resting heart rate is 72 bpm.

entries.text: Photosynthesis is the process by which plants, algae, and some bacteria use sunlight, water, and carbon dioxide to make sugar and release oxygen. It is the main way energy from the Sun enters almost all food chains on Earth.
entries.example: 6 CO₂ + 6 H₂O + light energy → C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6 O₂ is the overall equation for photosynthesis.

entries.text: Evolution is the gradual change in the inherited traits of a population of living things over many generations. Individuals with traits that help them survive and reproduce in their environment tend to pass those traits on more often, which is called natural selection.
entries.example: Over generations, moths in polluted areas became darker because dark moths were harder for birds to spot.

entries.text: An ecosystem is a community of living things, such as plants, animals, and microbes, together with the non-living parts of their environment, like water, soil, and air, all interacting with each other. Energy flows through an ecosystem and nutrients are recycled within it.
entries.example: A coral reef, a forest, and a pond are each their own ecosystem.

entries.text: A way to write a function as an infinite sum of powers of (x − a), built from the function's derivatives at one point a. Each added term makes the sum match the function better near that point; a Maclaurin series is the special case a = 0. The general form is f(x) = Σ f⁽ⁿ⁾(a)(x − a)ⁿ / n!.
The rate of change of a function with several inputs when only one input changes and the others are held fixed. It is written ∂f/∂x, where the curly ∂ means 'partial'.
entries.example: For f(x, y) = x²y, ∂f/∂x = 2xy.

entries.text: A shortcut for limits that give 0/0 or ∞/∞: differentiate the top and the bottom separately, then take the limit of that new ratio. It only applies when the original limit is one of these indeterminate forms.
entries.example: lim(x→0) sin x / x is 0/0; differentiating gives cos x / 1, which approaches 1.

entries.text: An integral over an interval that goes on forever, or one where the function blows up inside the interval. You evaluate it as a limit of ordinary integrals: if the limit is a finite number it converges, otherwise it diverges.
entries.example: ∫₁^∞ 1/x² dx = 1, so it converges.

entries.text: A rule for checking whether an infinite series Σaₙ converges, using L = lim(n→∞) |aₙ₊₁ / aₙ|. If L < 1 the series converges, if L > 1 it diverges, and if L = 1 the test gives no answer.
entries.example: For Σ 1/n!, the ratio is 1/(n+1), which goes to 0, so the series converges.

entries.text: The logarithm with base e (about 2.71828), written ln x. It answers the question 'what power of e gives x?', so ln(eˣ) = x and e^(ln x) = x.
entries.example: ln(e³) = 3 and ln(1) = 0.

entries.text: A function that raises the constant e (about 2.71828) to the input power, written eˣ or exp(x). It is its own derivative, d/dx eˣ = eˣ, which is why it models continuous growth so well.

A method for finding dy/dx when y is tied to x by an equation but is not isolated as y = f(x). You differentiate both sides with respect to x, multiply each y-term by dy/dx using the chain rule, and then solve for dy/dx.
entries.example: For x² + y² = 25, 2x + 2y·dy/dx = 0, so dy/dx = −x/y.

entries.text: Problems where several quantities change over time and are linked by an equation. You differentiate that equation with respect to time t, usually with implicit differentiation, then plug in the known values to find the unknown rate.
entries.example: For a sphere, V = (4/3)πr³ gives dV/dt = 4πr² · dr/dt.

entries.text: An estimate of the area under a curve made by adding the areas of many thin rectangles. Each rectangle has width Δx = (b − a)/n and a height taken from the function at a sample point, and the sum approaches the exact integral as n grows.
entries.example: Four left rectangles for ∫₀² x² dx give 1.75, while the exact value is 8/3 ≈ 2.67.

entries.text: The amount of space between a graph and the x-axis over a given interval. Area above the axis counts as positive and area below counts as negative, and it is found exactly with the definite integral ∫ₐᵇ f(x) dx.
entries.example: Under y = 2x from x = 0 to 3, the area is 9, which is a triangle with base 3 and height 6.

entries.text: A buffer is a solution that resists big changes in pH when small amounts of acid or base are added. It is made from a weak acid and its conjugate base (or a weak base and its conjugate acid).
entries.example: Blood is buffered to stay near pH 7.4, so a small amount of acid from exercise does not make it dangerously acidic.

entries.text: Titration is a lab method where a solution of known concentration is added slowly to another solution until the reaction is just complete. The measured volume used lets you calculate the unknown concentration.
entries.example: Adding sodium hydroxide from a burette to vinegar until the color changes shows how much acetic acid the vinegar contains.

entries.text: An indicator is a substance that changes color at a specific pH or chemical condition, showing when a reaction has reached its endpoint. It is usually a weak dye that is added in small amounts.
entries.example: Phenolphthalein is colorless in acid and turns pink in base.

entries.text: An endothermic reaction absorbs heat from its surroundings, so the surroundings get colder. Its enthalpy change is positive (ΔH > 0).
entries.example: Dissolving ammonium nitrate in water makes the water feel cold.

entries.text: An exothermic reaction releases heat into its surroundings, so the surroundings get warmer. Its enthalpy change is negative (ΔH < 0).
entries.example: Burning wood or the reaction inside a hand warmer releases heat.

entries.text: Combustion is a rapid reaction of a substance with oxygen that releases heat and usually light. Burning a hydrocarbon produces carbon dioxide and water.
entries.example: CH₄ + 2O₂ → CO₂ + 2H₂O is the combustion of methane in a gas stove.

entries.text: Reaction rate is how fast reactants are used up or products are formed, measured as a change in concentration per unit time, in mol·L⁻¹·s⁻¹. Temperature, concentration, surface area and catalysts can all change it.
entries.example: A tablet dissolves faster in hot water than in cold water because the reaction rate is higher.

entries.text: Chemical equilibrium is the state where the forward and reverse reactions happen at the same rate, so the concentrations stop changing overall. The reaction has not stopped; the changes just cancel out.
entries.example: In a closed bottle of soda, the rate of CO₂ leaving the liquid equals the rate of it re-entering, so the fizz level stays steady.

entries.text: Solubility is the maximum amount of a substance (the solute) that can dissolve in a given amount of solvent at a given temperature. It is often given in grams per 100 g of water or in mol/L.
entries.example: About 36 g of table salt dissolves in 100 g of water at 20 °C.

entries.text: ppm, or parts per million, is a concentration unit meaning one part of solute for every million parts of the whole mixture. For dilute water it equals 1 mg per liter.
entries.example: A fluoride level of 1 ppm means there is 1 mg of fluoride in each liter of water.

entries.text: Valence electrons are the electrons in an atom's outermost shell. They are the electrons that take part in chemical bonding.
entries.example: Carbon has 4 valence electrons, which is why it forms four bonds in methane.

entries.text: The ideal gas law says PV = nRT, linking a gas's pressure P, volume V, amount n in moles and temperature T in kelvin. R = 8.314 J·mol⁻¹·K⁻¹ is the gas constant.
entries.example: At 273 K and 1 atm, one mole of gas occupies about 22.4 L.

entries.text: Stoichiometry uses the coefficients of a balanced chemical equation as mole ratios to work out how much reactant is needed or how much product forms. It turns the equation into quantities you can measure.
entries.example: In 2H₂ + O₂ → 2H₂O, 2 mol of hydrogen reacts with 1 mol of oxygen to make 2 mol of water.

entries.text: Monthly recurring revenue is the predictable money a subscription business expects to collect each month from its paying customers. It is calculated as MRR = number of paying customers × average monthly fee per customer.
entries.example: 100 customers paying $50 a month gives an MRR of $5,000.

entries.text: Annual recurring revenue is the yearly value of a company's subscriptions, found by multiplying MRR by 12 (ARR = MRR × 12). It is the standard way to measure how big a subscription business is.
entries.example: An MRR of $5,000 means an ARR of $60,000.

entries.text: Churn rate is the share of customers (or revenue) lost over a set period, calculated as customers lost ÷ customers at the start of the period × 100%. A high churn rate means people are leaving faster than new ones arrive.
entries.example: Losing 20 of 400 customers in one month is a 5% monthly churn rate.

entries.text: Lifetime value is the total profit a business expects to earn from one customer over the whole time they stay. A common estimate is LTV = ARPU × gross margin ÷ churn rate, so it shows what a customer is worth in the long run.
entries.example: A customer paying $50 a month, with 80% gross margin and 5% monthly churn, has an LTV of about $50 × 0.8 ÷ 0.05 = $800.

entries.text: Customer acquisition cost is how much a company spends on sales and marketing to win one new paying customer. It is calculated as total acquisition spending ÷ number of new customers won.
entries.example: Spending $10,000 on ads and sales to win 50 customers gives a CAC of $200.

entries.text: Runway is how many months a company can keep operating before it runs out of cash. It is calculated as cash on hand ÷ monthly net burn rate.
entries.example: $480,000 in the bank with a $40,000 monthly net burn gives 12 months of runway.

entries.text: Net margin is the percentage of revenue that is left as profit after every expense is paid, including rent, salaries, interest and taxes. It is calculated as net income ÷ revenue × 100%.
entries.example: A company with $1,000,000 in revenue and $80,000 in net income has an 8% net margin.

terms: earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation, and amortization
entries.text: EBITDA measures a company's profit from its core operations before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortization are subtracted. It is calculated as operating profit + depreciation + amortization, and it is often used to compare businesses.
entries.example: A company with $200,000 in operating profit and $30,000 in depreciation has an EBITDA of $230,000.

entries.text: A cohort is a group of customers who share a starting point, such as signing up in the same month. Cohort analysis tracks how each group behaves over time, to see whether newer customers stick around better than older ones.
entries.example: All users who signed up in January form the January cohort.

entries.text: Retention rate is the share of customers from the start of a period who are still active at the end of it. It is calculated as (customers at end − new customers added) ÷ customers at start × 100%, and it is the mirror image of churn rate.
entries.example: Keeping 380 of 400 customers over a month is a 95% retention rate.

entries.text: A funnel is the series of steps people go through on the way to a goal, such as visit, sign up, try and pay. It is drawn as stages that get narrower because fewer people reach each one, which helps teams find where most people drop off.
entries.example: 1,000 visitors, 200 sign-ups and 40 paying customers make a three-step funnel.

entries.text: Conversion rate is the percentage of visitors or leads who complete a desired action, such as buying or signing up. It is calculated as conversions ÷ total visitors × 100%.
entries.example: 40 buyers out of 1,000 visitors is a 4% conversion rate.

entries.text: ARPU is the average amount of money a company earns from each user in a given period. It is calculated as total revenue ÷ number of users for that period.
entries.example: $50,000 in monthly revenue from 2,000 users gives an ARPU of $25 per month.

entries.text: Net Promoter Score measures customer loyalty by asking how likely people are to recommend a business on a 0 to 10 scale. It is the percentage of promoters (scores 9 to 10) minus the percentage of detractors (scores 0 to 6), giving a result from −100 to +100.
entries.example: If 50% of customers are promoters and 10% are detractors, the NPS is +40.

entries.text: Daily active users is the number of unique people who use a product on a given day. It shows how many people come back in the short term.
entries.example: If 3,000 different people open an app today, its DAU is 3,000.

entries.text: Monthly active users is the number of unique people who use a product at least once during a calendar month. Dividing DAU by MAU gives a stickiness ratio, which shows how often monthly users return each day.
entries.example: A product with 10,000 DAU and 40,000 MAU has a DAU/MAU ratio of 0.25.

entries.text: Unit economics is the profit a business makes on one unit of what it sells, such as one customer, and it asks whether each sale pays for itself. Common checks compare LTV to CAC and look at the payback period.
entries.example: A customer worth $800 in lifetime value who cost $200 to acquire gives an LTV to CAC ratio of 4 to 1, which is generally considered healthy.

entries.text: Payback period is the number of months it takes for a customer's gross profit to repay the cost of acquiring them. It is calculated as CAC ÷ (ARPU × gross margin), and shorter is better because cash comes back sooner.
entries.example: A $200 CAC with $50 monthly revenue at 80% gross margin pays back in 200 ÷ 40 = 5 months.

entries.text: The economic model of how prices get set. Buyers want more of a good when it is cheaper, sellers offer more when it sells for more, and the price settles where the amount buyers want matches the amount sellers offer.
entries.example: If many people want concert tickets but only a few are sold, the price rises until fewer buyers are willing to pay it.
