entries.text: How much of a product sellers are willing and able to offer at a given price. Sellers usually offer more when the price is higher.
entries.example: At $10 a bottle a shop might stock 50 bottles, but at $15 it might stock 80.

entries.text: How much of a product buyers want and can afford at a given price. Buyers usually want more when the price is lower.
entries.example: If a pizza costs $5, more people buy it than when it costs $20.

entries.text: A measure of how much the quantity people buy changes when the price changes. Formula: elasticity = (% change in quantity demanded) ÷ (% change in price). An absolute value bigger than 1 means buyers react strongly to price; a value between 0 and 1 means they barely react.
entries.example: If a 10% price rise cuts sales by 20%, the elasticity is −2, so buyers are sensitive to price.

entries.text: GDP measured at today's market prices, without adjusting for inflation. If prices double while output stays the same, nominal GDP doubles even though the economy did not grow.
GDP adjusted for inflation, so it measures the actual quantity of output at constant prices. Formula: real GDP = nominal GDP ÷ GDP deflator × 100.
entries.example: If nominal GDP rises 6% but prices rise 4%, real GDP grew about 2%.

entries.text: The decisions a central bank makes about its benchmark interest rate and related tools to steer the economy. Cutting rates encourages borrowing and spending to fight a slowdown; raising rates cools spending to fight inflation.
entries.example: If the central bank raises its benchmark rate from 2% to 4%, mortgage and loan costs rise and spending tends to slow.

entries.text: The extra cost of producing one more unit of a good. Formula: MC = change in total cost ÷ change in quantity.
entries.example: If making 100 mugs costs $500 and making 101 costs $505, the marginal cost of the 101st mug is $5.

entries.text: Cost savings a business gets as it produces more. The average cost per unit falls as output grows because fixed costs are spread over more units and bulk buying and specialization lower costs.
entries.example: A car factory that builds 1 million cars a year pays less per car for its plant and machines than one that builds 10,000.

entries.text: A market with only one seller of a product that has no close substitutes. Without competition, the seller can set prices higher than competition would allow.
entries.example: A town's only water utility, with no other company allowed to sell water there, is a monopoly.

entries.text: The percentage change in the general price level over a year, usually measured with a price index such as the consumer price index (CPI). Formula: inflation rate = (CPI now − CPI a year ago) ÷ CPI a year ago × 100%.
entries.example: If a basket of goods rises from a CPI of 300 to 306, the inflation rate is 2%.

entries.text: How much goods and services a unit of money can buy. It falls when prices rise and rises when prices fall. Formula: real value = nominal amount ÷ price index × 100.
entries.example: $100 buys 20 meals at $5 each, but if meals rise to $6, the same $100 buys only about 16.7.

entries.text: The price of one currency expressed in another currency. A stronger home currency makes imports and foreign travel cheaper, while a weaker one makes exports cheaper for foreign buyers.
entries.example: If 1 US dollar buys 0.90 euros, the exchange rate is 0.90 EUR per USD.

entries.text: Deployment is putting a new version of an application onto the servers or machines where real users reach it. Deploying takes code that has passed testing and makes it live.
entries.example: Copying version 2.4 of a web app onto production servers so customers start using it.

entries.text: A rollback sends a system back to a previous, known-working version after a bad release. It is usually the fastest way to undo a deployment that causes problems.
entries.example: After version 2.5 starts throwing errors, the team rolls back to version 2.4 within minutes.

entries.text: A canary release sends a new version to a small slice of users first, such as 1% or 5% of traffic, and watches it before rolling out to everyone. The name comes from the canary birds miners used to detect dangerous gas.
entries.example: Route 5% of requests to the new version; if error rates stay normal, raise it to 25%, then 100%.

entries.text: A feature flag is a switch in code or configuration that turns a feature on or off without redeploying. It lets teams ship code with a feature turned off and enable it later for some users or for everyone.
entries.example: A new checkout button ships hidden, and the team turns it on for employees first.

entries.text: CI/CD is an automated pipeline that builds code and runs tests on every change (continuous integration), then packages or ships the passing code automatically (continuous delivery or deployment). It turns releases into a repeatable machine process instead of a series of manual steps.
entries.example: Every push runs the unit tests, and passing builds are deployed to a staging server automatically.

entries.text: A container packages an application together with the libraries and settings it needs into one portable unit that runs the same way on any machine. Containers share the host's operating system kernel, so they start in seconds and use less memory than full virtual machines.
entries.example: A Docker image bundling a Python app and its dependencies runs the same on a laptop and on a cloud server.

entries.text: Kubernetes is an open-source system that runs and manages many containers across a cluster of machines. It starts, restarts, scales, and routes containers automatically according to rules you declare.
entries.example: You tell Kubernetes to keep 5 copies of a web service running, and if one crashes it starts a replacement.

entries.text: A load balancer sits in front of several servers and spreads incoming requests among them so that no single server is overloaded. It usually also stops sending traffic to servers that fail their health checks.
entries.example: Ten thousand requests per minute are split across four web servers, with each handling about 2,500.

entries.text: A circuit breaker stops a service from repeatedly calling another service that keeps failing. After enough failures it opens and fails fast without calling, then tries again after a cooldown so the broken service has time to recover.
entries.example: After 5 timeouts in 10 seconds calling the payment service, the breaker opens and returns an error immediately for 30 seconds.

entries.text: An operation is idempotent if doing it several times has the same effect as doing it once. This matters because retried requests can otherwise charge a card twice or create duplicate orders.
entries.example: Setting a user's email to a fixed value is idempotent, but adding 10 dollars to a balance is not unless the request carries a unique key.

entries.text: Observability is how well you can understand what is happening inside a running system by looking at the data it produces. It usually rests on three kinds of signals: logs, metrics, and traces.
entries.example: A dashboard shows the error rate rising, and a trace points to a slow database query as the cause.

entries.text: Distributed tracing follows a single request as it passes through many services and records how long each step took. Each step is a span, and the spans together form a trace that shows where the time went.
entries.example: A checkout request's trace shows 40 ms in the cart service and 900 ms waiting on the payment service.

entries.text: Logging means writing timestamped records of events a program is doing, such as errors, requests, or state changes. Logs help engineers find out what happened after something goes wrong.
entries.example: 2026-10-28 10:14:02 ERROR payment declined order_id=8812

entries.text: A CDN is a network of servers spread around the world that stores copies of static content such as images, videos, and scripts close to users. Users download from a nearby copy, which makes pages load faster and reduces load on the origin server.
entries.example: A user in Tokyo loads a product image from a Tokyo edge server instead of one in Virginia.

entries.text: DNS is the internet's phone book: it translates human-friendly domain names like example.com into the IP addresses that computers use to connect. Devices cache each answer for a period set by the record's TTL (time to live).
entries.example: Typing example.com makes your browser ask DNS, which replies with 203.0.113.10.

entries.text: An HTTP status code is a three-digit number a server sends back to say how a request went. The first digit groups them: 2xx means success, 3xx means redirect, 4xx means the client made an error, and 5xx means the server failed.
entries.example: 200 OK means success, 404 Not Found means the page does not exist, and 503 Service Unavailable means the server is down or overloaded.

entries.text: A timeout is the maximum time a program will wait for an operation, such as a network reply, before giving up and treating it as failed. Without timeouts, one stuck call can hold resources indefinitely.
entries.example: A service waits at most 2 seconds for a reply from the inventory service, then returns an error.

entries.text: Retry with backoff means trying a failed operation again after a wait that grows each time, such as 1 s, then 2 s, then 4 s, often with a small random jitter added. The growing gaps keep a struggling service from being flooded with retries.
entries.example: A failed upload retries after 1 s, then 2 s, then 4 s, and gives up after five tries.

entries.text: Machine learning is a way of building software that learns patterns from example data instead of following hand-written rules. You show the computer many examples, and it adjusts itself until it can make good predictions on new data.
entries.example: A spam filter that learns what spam looks like from thousands of emails already marked as spam or not spam.

entries.text: The training set is the part of your data a model learns from by adjusting its internal settings. It is usually the largest chunk, often 70 to 80 percent of the total.
entries.example: Showing 8,000 of 10,000 labeled photos to a model so it can learn to tell cats from dogs.

entries.text: The test set is a separate portion of data that the model never sees during training. It is used at the end to check how well the model works on new examples, which gives an honest score.
entries.example: Holding back 2,000 photos and using them only once to report the final accuracy.

entries.text: Overfitting happens when a model memorizes the quirks and noise of its training data so closely that it does poorly on new data. It is like a student who memorizes last year's exam answers and fails when the questions change.
entries.example: A model scores 99 percent on its training data but only 70 percent on the test set.

entries.text: Underfitting happens when a model is too simple to capture the real pattern in the data, so it does poorly on both training and new data. It is like drawing a straight line through points that clearly curve.
entries.example: Predicting house prices with a single flat average that ignores size and location.

entries.text: Precision is the share of the things a model labeled positive that really were positive. Formula: precision = TP ÷ (TP + FP), where TP is true positives and FP is false positives.
entries.example: If a spam filter flags 100 emails and 90 are really spam, precision is 90 percent.

entries.text: Recall is the share of all the real positives that the model successfully found. Formula: recall = TP ÷ (TP + FN), where FN is false negatives, the positives the model missed.
entries.example: If there are 50 fraud cases and the model catches 40 of them, recall is 80 percent.

entries.text: The F1 score is one number that balances precision and recall using their harmonic mean. Formula: F1 = 2 × (precision × recall) ÷ (precision + recall). It is high only when both precision and recall are high.
entries.example: Precision 0.9 and recall 0.5 give an F1 of about 0.64, which is lower than their simple average of 0.7.

entries.text: Accuracy is the fraction of all predictions the model got right. Formula: accuracy = (TP + TN) ÷ total predictions. It can be misleading when one class is very rare.
entries.example: A model that always says not fraud is 99 percent accurate if only 1 percent of transactions are fraud, yet it catches no fraud at all.

entries.text: A confusion matrix is a table that counts each kind of correct and incorrect prediction. Actual labels run down one side and predicted labels run across the top. For two classes it has four cells: true positives, true negatives, false positives and false negatives.
entries.example: A 2×2 table showing 40 true positives, 5 false positives, 10 false negatives and 945 true negatives.

entries.text: A classifier is a model that sorts inputs into named categories, such as spam or not spam. Its final answer is a label, though many classifiers also compute a probability score for each label.
entries.example: A model that reads an email and answers urgent or not urgent.

entries.text: A regression model predicts a continuous number, such as a price, temperature or height, rather than a category. It learns how the inputs relate to that number.
entries.example: Predicting a house's price in dollars from its size and number of bedrooms.

entries.text: A feature is one measurable input the model uses to make a prediction, like a column in a spreadsheet. Good features describe a situation in a way that helps the model tell the possible answers apart.
entries.example: For house prices, square footage, number of bedrooms and postcode are all features.

entries.text: Gradient descent is the method models use to improve by repeatedly nudging their settings a small step in the direction that lowers the error. The direction comes from the gradient, which is the slope of the error with respect to each setting.
entries.example: Like walking downhill in fog by feeling the slope under your feet and taking small steps down.

entries.text: A neural network is a model built from layers of simple connected units, called neurons. Each neuron combines its inputs using adjustable weights and passes the result on. Stacking many layers lets the network learn complex patterns such as faces or speech.
entries.example: A network that takes in pixel values and outputs cat or dog after passing through several hidden layers.

entries.text: Cross-validation tests a model more reliably by splitting the data into several parts, called folds. The model is trained and tested on different combinations of folds, and the scores are averaged. With k = 5 folds, each fold serves as the test set once.
entries.example: Splitting 1,000 rows into 5 folds of 200 rows, getting five scores, and averaging them.

entries.text: Anomaly detection finds data points that are unusual compared with the normal pattern, often without labeled examples of the unusual cases. It is used to spot things like fraud, equipment failure or network intrusions.
entries.example: Flagging a $9,000 credit card charge when the cardholder usually spends under $50.

entries.text: A time series is data recorded in order over time, such as a stock price each day or a temperature each hour. Because nearby points are related, forecasting models use the order of the data and its past values to predict what comes next.
entries.example: Daily website visits over a year, used to forecast next week's traffic.

entries.text: The digits in a number that show its precision, counted from the first non-zero digit. Leading zeros never count, but zeros after the first non-zero digit usually do when a decimal point is present.
entries.example: 3.2050 has 5 significant figures, and 0.0720 has 3.

entries.text: Replacing a number with a nearby simpler value, such as the nearest whole number or tenth, so it is easier to read or use. Look at the digit just after the place you are keeping: 5 or more rounds up, 4 or less rounds down.
entries.example: 3.46 rounded to one decimal place is 3.5.

entries.text: Finding a quick, approximate answer by swapping numbers for easier nearby values and doing rough mental arithmetic. It tells you whether an exact answer is in a sensible range.
entries.example: 198 × 52 is about 200 × 50 = 10,000; the exact answer is 10,296.

entries.text: How much a quantity went up or down, as a percentage of its original value. Formula: percent change = (new − old) ÷ old × 100%. A rise gives a positive result and a fall gives a negative one.
The simple difference between two percentages, written as pp. It measures how far a rate moved, not how much it changed relative to its starting value.
entries.example: Unemployment falls from 6% to 5%: that is a fall of 1 percentage point, but a percent change of about −16.7%.

entries.text: Growth where each period's increase is added to the total before the next period, so earlier growth also grows. Formula: final = start × (1 + r)ⁿ, where r is the rate per period as a decimal and n is the number of periods.
entries.example: £100 growing 10% a year for 2 years: 100 × 1.1² = £121.

entries.text: A ratio compares two or more quantities of the same kind, written a:b. A proportion says two ratios are equal, meaning the quantities scale together in a fixed way.
entries.example: Paint mixed 2:3 (blue to white): 4 litres of blue needs 6 litres of white, because 2:3 = 4:6.

entries.text: A rate expressed per one unit of something, which makes two different amounts easy to compare. Formula: unit rate = total ÷ number of units.
entries.example: A 500 g pack costs £2.50, so the unit rate is £2.50 ÷ 500 g = £0.005 per gram, or 0.5p per gram.

entries.text: The total distance travelled divided by the total time taken, regardless of how speed changed along the way. Formula: average speed = distance ÷ time, in units such as km/h or m/s.
entries.example: Driving 120 km in 2 hours gives an average speed of 60 km/h, even if you went faster at times.

entries.text: A whole number written together with a proper fraction, such as 2 3/4, meaning 2 + 3/4. Its value sits between two whole numbers.
entries.example: 2 3/4 means 2 + 3/4, which is 2.75.

entries.text: A fraction whose numerator is equal to or larger than its denominator, so its value is 1 or more. To convert a mixed number: multiply the whole part by the denominator, add the numerator, and keep the same denominator.
Writing a whole number greater than 1 as a product of prime numbers only. Apart from the order of the factors, each such number has exactly one prime factorisation.
entries.example: 60 = 2 × 2 × 3 × 5, which can be written 2² × 3 × 5.

entries.text: The result of multiplying a whole number by itself three times, written n³. Geometrically, it is the volume of a cube with side length n. The first few are 1, 8, 27, 64.
A number less than zero, written with a minus sign, such as −4. On a number line it sits to the left of zero. Multiplying two negatives gives a positive, and adding a negative moves you left.

The agreed sequence for evaluating an expression: brackets first, then powers (indices), then multiplication and division from left to right, then addition and subtraction from left to right. Mnemonics: BIDMAS or BODMAS.
entries.example: 2 + 3 × 4 = 14, not 20, because the multiplication is done first.

entries.text: p99 latency is the response time that 99 out of every 100 requests beat, so the slowest 1% take at least this long. It shows the experience of the unluckiest users, which averages and p95 can hide.
entries.example: If p99 latency is 2.4 s, then 1 in 100 requests takes 2.4 s or longer.

entries.text: MTTD is the average time between when a problem begins and when the team notices it, usually through an alert or a customer report. Shorter detection means less damage happens before anyone responds.
entries.example: If a problem starts at 10:00 and an alert fires at 10:12, that incident's detection time is 12 minutes.

entries.text: A true positive is a case where a test or alert correctly signals that a real problem exists. In monitoring, it is an alert that fires during a genuine incident.
entries.example: The checkout alert fires at 3 a.m. because checkout is really failing, so it is a true positive.

entries.text: Saturation measures how full a resource is, such as CPU, memory, disk, a connection pool or a queue, and how much work is waiting because the resource cannot keep up. A system near saturation slows down sharply, even when its average throughput still looks fine.
entries.example: A database connection pool with 98 of 100 connections in use and requests queuing is near saturation.

entries.text: The four golden signals are key measurements for watching a user-facing service: latency (how long requests take), traffic (how much demand there is), errors (how often requests fail) and saturation (how full the system is). Together they give a quick picture of health.
entries.example: A dashboard showing p99 latency, requests per second, the 5xx error rate and CPU use covers all four signals.

contrasts.text: Perimeter measures the length of the boundary of a 2D shape, while area measures the flat space inside it.
Radius runs from the center out to the edge, while diameter runs straight across through the center and is twice as long.
Surface area counts the square units covering the outside of a 3D solid, while volume counts the cubic units of space it fills.
Equity makes you a part-owner who shares in a company's profits and losses, while a bond makes you a lender who is owed regular interest and repayment of the face value.
An annuity is the fixed series of payments itself, while amortisation is the process of paying a debt down through those payments.
A recession is a sustained fall in total economic output (real GDP), while deflation is a sustained fall in the general price level.
ROI is a percentage gain relative to what was spent, while NPV is a dollar amount in today's money after discounting future cash flows.
Charge is the quantity of electricity, measured in coulombs, while current is how fast that charge flows, measured in amperes.

In a series circuit the same current passes through every component and the voltage is shared between them, while in a parallel circuit every branch gets the full voltage and the current splits between the branches.
A watt measures power, the rate at which energy is used, while a kilowatt-hour measures energy itself, so it equals power multiplied by time.
An electric field pushes on any charge, moving or still, and comes from electric charges, while a magnetic field only pushes on moving charges and comes from magnets or currents.
An atom is a single particle of an element, while a molecule is a group of atoms bonded together.
An element has only one kind of atom, while a compound has two or more different elements bonded in a fixed ratio.
An ion differs in electric charge because it gained or lost electrons, while an isotope differs in neutron count and keeps the same charge.
A covalent bond shares electrons between atoms, while an ionic bond transfers electrons so the resulting ions attract each other.
The domain is the set of allowed inputs (x-values), while the range is the set of outputs (y-values) the function actually produces.
The arithmetic mean adds the values and divides by how many there are, while the geometric mean multiplies the values and takes the nth root, so it suits growth factors instead of plain amounts.
A coefficient is the number multiplying a variable (the 3 in 3x), while a constant is a fixed number with no variable attached (the 7 in 3x + 7).
A scalar is a single number with only a size, while a vector has both a size and a direction.
Distance is the total length of the path travelled, while displacement is only the straight-line change from start to finish, including direction.
Work is the energy transferred by a force, while power is how quickly that work is done, measured in watts (W = J/s).
Frequency counts how many cycles pass each second (in hertz), while wavelength measures the length of one full cycle in space (in metres).
Gravity is the attractive pull between masses in general, while weight is the specific force gravity exerts on one object, equal to its mass times g (W = m·g).
Latency is how long one request takes to finish, while throughput is how many requests finish per unit of time.
A bit is a single 0 or 1, while a byte is a group of 8 bits, so network speeds are usually quoted in bits and file sizes in bytes.
Hashing is one-way and produces a fixed-size fingerprint, while encryption is reversible with a key so the original data can be recovered.
Bandwidth is the maximum capacity a connection can carry, while throughput is the amount actually delivered in practice, which is usually lower.
A sample is the part you actually measure, while the population is the whole group you want to learn about.
The mean is the average of data you have already collected, while the expected value is the average you predict over many random outcomes, weighted by their probabilities.
Correlation only measures how strongly two quantities move together in a straight-line way, from -1 to 1, while regression goes further and predicts one from the other using a line.
A hypothesis test is the whole decision procedure, while the p-value is the single number it produces to show how surprising the data would be if the null hypothesis were true.
An SLA is the external promise to customers, with penalties if it is broken, while an SLO is the internal target the team actually aims for, usually set stricter than the SLA.
An SLI is the measurement of how the service is really performing, while an SLO is the target that measurement is judged against.
A false positive is an alarm with no real problem behind it, while a false negative is a real problem that raises no alarm.
A tangent line touches a curve at a point and has the curve's exact slope there, while a secant line cuts through two points on the curve and has the average slope between them.
A definite integral is a single number (the signed area between two x-values), while an antiderivative is a function whose derivative is the original function.
The chain rule differentiates a function nested inside another, f(g(x)), while the product rule differentiates two functions multiplied together, f(x) · g(x).
A local maximum is a peak where the curve switches from rising to falling, while an inflection point is where the curve switches between bending up and bending down.
Probability is the chance of an event out of all possible outcomes, while odds compare the chance it happens with the chance it doesn't. A probability of 0.8 corresponds to odds of 4 to 1.
A type I error rejects a true null hypothesis (a false positive), while a type II error fails to reject a false null hypothesis (a false negative). Lowering one usually raises the other.
Covariance shows the direction of a relationship but its size depends on the units of the variables. Correlation is covariance rescaled to run from −1 to 1, so it measures strength on a common scale.

Standard deviation describes how spread out the individual values in one sample are. Standard error describes how much a sample statistic, such as the mean, would vary across repeated samples, and it shrinks as the sample grows.
Conditional probability is the chance of A given that B happened, which is generally different from P(A). Independent events are the special case where knowing B leaves the chance of A unchanged.
The standard deviation uses every value and is pulled strongly by outliers. The interquartile range uses only the middle 50% of the data, so it is more robust to extreme values.
A union keeps everything that is in either set, while an intersection keeps only what is in both.
An eigenvalue is the number λ by which a matrix scales a vector, while an eigenvector is the vector v whose direction is preserved.
A dot product gives a single number in any dimension, while a cross product gives a new vector perpendicular to both inputs and is standardly defined only for 3D vectors.
A graph can have loops and be disconnected, while a tree is a connected graph with no cycles.
Proof by contradiction assumes the claim is false and reaches an impossibility, while proof by induction proves the claim for all cases by a base case and a step that passes it along.
Modular arithmetic is the wrap-around system of working with remainders, while congruence is the statement a ≡ b (mod n) that two numbers share a remainder.
Temperature is how hot something is, while heat is the energy that flows between objects because they have different temperatures. A small object can have a high temperature but store little heat.
Reflection is a wave bouncing back off a surface, while refraction is a wave bending as it passes into a different material. Both happen to light at the same boundary.

Heat is the energy that moves, while specific heat capacity is a property of a material that says how much energy it takes to warm 1 kg of it by 1 K. Heat is the quantity transferred, and specific heat capacity helps calculate it.
Radioactivity is the process of unstable nuclei emitting radiation, while half-life is the time it takes for half of those nuclei to decay. Half-life measures how fast radioactivity fades.
Buoyancy is the general upward push a fluid exerts on an object, while Archimedes' principle is the rule that gives the size of that push: the weight of the displaced fluid.
A gravitational field describes the pull a mass exerts at each point in space, measured in N/kg. Escape velocity is the speed needed to get out of that field completely from a planet's surface.
A virus is not a cell and cannot reproduce on its own, so it must invade a host cell to multiply. Bacteria are living single-celled organisms that reproduce by themselves.
DNA is the whole long molecule that stores all of an organism's instructions. A gene is one specific segment of that DNA that codes for a particular protein or function.
A gene is the blueprint written in DNA, while a protein is the molecule built from that blueprint. Genes are instructions; proteins are the working parts that carry them out.

A vaccine is a substance you receive to train your immune system to make antibodies against a germ. An antibody is the protein the immune system actually produces to attach to and neutralize that germ.
Every enzyme is a protein, but not every protein is an enzyme. An enzyme is a protein whose specific job is to speed up a chemical reaction, while other proteins build structures or carry substances.

Metabolism is the whole set of chemical processes in a body that turns food into energy and builds new material. A calorie is only a unit used to measure how much energy those processes release or food contains.
A derivative measures change in a function of one variable. A partial derivative does the same for a function of several variables, changing only one input while holding the rest fixed.
A partial derivative is a single rate of change along one input. The gradient gathers all the partial derivatives into one vector that points in the steepest direction.
A Riemann sum is a finite sum of rectangle areas that approximates the area under a curve. The integral is the exact value that these sums approach as the rectangles get thinner.
A logarithm can use any base. The natural logarithm ln x always uses base e, so it is the logarithm with base e.

The exponential function eˣ is a specific mathematical function with base e. Exponential growth is a pattern in which a quantity increases by a fixed percentage over equal time steps, and eˣ is one way to model it.

The chain rule is the basic rule for differentiating a function inside another function. Implicit differentiation applies the chain rule to both sides of an equation where y is not written alone, so the derivative dy/dx can be solved for.
An endothermic reaction absorbs heat and makes its surroundings colder, while an exothermic reaction releases heat and makes its surroundings warmer.
Titration is the whole lab procedure of adding a known solution until a reaction is complete, while an indicator is the dye that changes color to show that completion point during a titration.
Valence electrons are the actual outer-shell electrons of an atom that take part in bonding, while an oxidation state is a bookkeeping number that tracks electron gain or loss in a compound.
Reaction rate is how fast a reaction proceeds, while chemical equilibrium is the state where forward and reverse reactions balance so concentrations stop changing overall.
Solubility is the maximum amount of a solute that can dissolve in a solvent at a given temperature, while ppm is a unit used to express how concentrated a mixture is.

Combustion is a specific type of reaction in which a substance reacts rapidly with oxygen, while exothermic describes any reaction that releases heat; combustion is always exothermic, but not every exothermic reaction is combustion.
MRR is the recurring revenue for one month, while ARR is the same revenue annualized over a full year, so ARR = MRR × 12.

Gross margin subtracts only the direct costs of delivering what you sell, while net margin subtracts every expense, including overhead, interest and taxes, so net margin is usually the smaller of the two.
Churn rate measures the share of customers lost over a period, while retention rate measures the share kept; together they add up to 100%.
Burn rate is how fast a company spends its cash each month, while runway is how many months that cash will last at that burn rate.
CAC is the cost to win one new customer, while LTV is the total profit that customer brings over their whole relationship, and a business is healthy when LTV is clearly higher than CAC.
DAU counts unique users active on a single day, while MAU counts unique users active at least once in a month, so MAU is always at least as large as DAU.
Nominal GDP uses current prices, so it rises with inflation as well as output. Real GDP strips out price changes, so it shows whether the economy actually produced more.
Opportunity cost is the value of the best alternative you give up when choosing. Marginal cost is the extra cost to a producer of making one more unit.
Supply is how much sellers are willing to offer at a price. Demand is how much buyers want to buy at that price. Supply and demand together set the market price.
Supply and demand is the model of how a price is set. Price elasticity measures how much the quantity bought or sold changes when the price changes.
Purchasing power is how much your money buys within your own country. The exchange rate is the price of your currency in another currency.
A deployment is the act of putting a new version onto servers. A canary release is a strategy for deploying, where the new version first reaches only a small share of users.
A rollback reverts the whole system to an earlier version, usually by deploying it again. A feature flag turns one feature off in the running system without any redeploy.
Logging is one tool that records events as text. Observability is the broader ability to understand a system's state from its logs, metrics, and traces together.
DNS turns a domain name into an address before any connection happens. A load balancer spreads requests across several servers after they arrive.
Retry with backoff keeps trying a failed call, waiting longer each time. A circuit breaker stops calls to a failing service entirely after repeated failures, so requests fail fast.
Idempotency is a property of an operation: repeating it has the same effect as doing it once. Retry with backoff is a strategy that is only safe to use on operations that are idempotent.

Precision asks how many of the model's positive predictions were correct, while recall asks how many of the real positives it found. A spam filter with high precision rarely flags good email; high recall means it catches most of the spam.
An overfit model learns noise and does well on training data but poorly on new data. An underfit model is too simple and does poorly on both.
The training set is used to learn the model's settings. The test set is held back and used only to check how well the finished model performs.
A classifier predicts a category, such as yes or no. A regression model predicts a continuous number, such as a price.
Accuracy counts all correct predictions, both positive and negative, out of all predictions. Precision looks only at the predictions labeled positive and asks how many of those were right.
A single test set gives one score from one split of the data. Cross-validation rotates through several splits and averages the scores, so the estimate is less dependent on one lucky or unlucky split.

Percent change is the relative change from the starting value, so it depends on the base. A percentage point is the plain difference between two percentages, so going from 10% to 13% is a rise of 3 percentage points but a 30% percent change.

Rounding applies a fixed rule to a specific number to cut it to a chosen place. Estimation approximates the result of a whole calculation by swapping in easier numbers, so the answer is only a rough guide.

Significant figures describe how precise a number is by counting its meaningful digits. Rounding is the action of cutting digits off, and you often round a number to a chosen count of significant figures.
A square number is n × n (two multiplications, area of a square). A cube number is n × n × n (three multiplications, volume of a cube). For example, 4 is a square number and 8 is a cube number.
A ratio is a comparison of two quantities, such as 2:3. A proportion goes further and states that two ratios are equal, such as 2:3 = 4:6.
A mixed number and an improper fraction can have the same value but are written differently. 2 3/4 is a mixed number, and 11/4 is the improper fraction for the same amount.
The error budget is the total unreliability allowed in the window. Burn rate is how fast that budget is being spent right now.
MTTD measures how long it takes to notice a problem. MTTR measures how long it takes to restore service, from the start of the incident to recovery.
A true positive is an alert that correctly fires for a real problem. A false negative is a real problem that never triggers an alert.
A runbook is written before an incident and tells responders what to do during one. A postmortem is written after an incident and explains what happened and how to prevent a repeat.
